title: Integration Architect Pegboard and Competitive Risk Scorecard – Sales Toolkit
author: Jordan Kim
body:
Overview
--------
This playbook is designed for sales engineers, solution architects, and field GTM teams who are engaging with platform/integration architects at mid-market and enterprise accounts. It combines: (1) a compact positioning pegboard (one-slide set of hooks that map to integration requirements), (2) a competitive risk scorecard that can be shown in technical due-diligence, (3) pricing guidance for pilot → scale, and (4) a short customer case study and security FAQ to accelerate approvals. Use this as the canonical single-page briefing for pre-demo calls and architecture workshops.

Who should use this
- Solution Engineers running technical discovery with platform/integration architects
- AEs preparing for procurement security meetings
- Customer Success teams onboarding pilots that need fast risk-reduction artifacts

One-line positioning (for the technical audience)
Redwood Inference provides a unified runtime for production LLM inference that lets platform teams preserve latency SLOs, control unit economics with intelligent batching and quantization profiles, and maintain consistent operational tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Top three integration hooks (pegboard)
1) Consistency across environments
   - Problem: Organizations run models in multiple environments (dev, hosted prod, on-prem regulated).
   - Redwood hook: single API and rollout controls so engineers don’t rewrite inference logic per environment.
   - What to show: model-version pinning example, canary rollout config, and a sample SDK call that works in-hosted and in-VPC.

2) Predictable economics and telemetry
   - Problem: Token cost and tail latency variability break budgeting and user experience.
   - Redwood hook: token-level cost traces, per-route latency budgets, and Optimize suggestions that estimate unit-cost impact before rollouts.
   - What to show: cost per 1k tokens by model/quantization (sample table below) and an exported trace from Console showing per-token breakdown.

3) Resilience and graceful degradation
   - Problem: Outages or capacity pressure cause noisy errors or bad fallbacks.
   - Redwood hook: smart routing + model-variant fallback policies and automatic KV-prefix caching.
   - What to show: route policy DSL snippet and canary → fallback example sequence.

Competitive risk scorecard (how to use)
- Purpose: a concise, technical comparison to bring into architectural reviews where procurement or security asks for tradeoffs. Present as a 1x1 slide and provide the driving evidence.
- Scoring: 0–3 for each category (0 = weak/dangerous, 3 = strong/enterprise-ready).

Sample scorecard (explainers included)
| Category | Redwood | Vendor A (closed-prop) | Vendor B (self-hosted only) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private) | 3 | 2 | 1 | Redwood offers unified control plane + private on-prem package. |
| Rollout controls / model versioning | 3 | 1 | 2 | Lightweight pinning and automated canaries. |
| Predictable latency at 99th % | 3 | 2 | 1 | Smart routing + autoscaling in dedicated pools. |
| Cost tooling (token telemetry, Optimize) | 3 | 1 | 2 | Token-level cost visibility + suggestions. |
| Privacy & compliance (KMS/HSM, audit logs) | 3 | 2 | 2 | Full KMS integrations and audit pipelines available for Private. |
| Multi-region redundancy | 2 | 3 | 1 | Redwood has region routing; vendor A offers multi-region global SLA. |
| Developer experience (SDKs, quickstarts) | 3 | 1 | 2 | Focus on fast onboarding and example apps. |
| Overall technical risk (lower is better) | 1 | 2 | 2 | Aggregate risk index (1–3). |

How to defend the scoring in conversations
- Be explicit about data sources: internal benchmarks, customer case metrics, and publicly disclosed vendor limitations.
- If asked about Vendor A’s higher multi-region score, pivot to the tradeoff (Vendor A replicates state vs Redwood’s smart routing + failover to compatible variants).

Pricing guidance: pilot → scale (recommended structure)
- Pilot (8–12 weeks): low friction, 2–3 model variants, usage cap with overage alerts. Suggested commercial: 3-month credit + capped usage pricing.
  - Example: included $6k platform credit + $0.0012 equivalent/token billable after credit.
  - Goals: validate latency under representative load, confirm cost per 1k tokens, run quality regression tests.
- Initial production (first 6 months): committed throughput slab for Dedicated or burst-capacity for hosted. Suggested: monthly commit covering baseline QPS and a growth buffer of 25%.
  - Example: committed plan for 200 A100-equivalent GPU-hours / month + usage overage at blended rate.
- Enterprise scale (12+ months): custom reserved capacity or Private licensing with multi-year commits, plus professional services for on-prem integration and compliance attestation.

Negotiation guardrails for SEs
1) Always align pilot SLAs with the customer’s acceptance criteria (latency, throughput, and cost thresholds).
2) Avoid open indefinite credits—tie credits to a clear technical milestone (e.g., 99th % latency < 800ms for canonical workload).
3) Preserve optionality in contracts to move from hosted → dedicated → private without rework on the application layer.

Sample slide bullets for a 6-slide pitch to platform architects
- Slide 1: Problem statement — inconsistent inference across environments and unpredictable unit economics.
- Slide 2: Redwood technical thesis — unified runtime + smart routing + per-token telemetry.
- Slide 3: Architecture sketch (hosted/dedicated/private) with failover paths.
- Slide 4: Cost/latency evidence (sample numbers and the Optimize recommendation preview).
- Slide 5: Integration playbook — SDK snippet, rollout config, and canary.
- Slide 6: Risk mitigation & next steps — pilot design and security checklist.

Customer case (short) — Fintech payments processor
- Context: mid-market payments company processing real-time risk scoring and fraud rules with <350ms median latency requirement.
- Pilot configuration: hosted runway + dedicated burst (4-week pilot), two model variants (small quantized LM + optimized medium LM), prefix caching for repeated user prompts.
- Outcomes: 42% reduction in median token cost vs previous self-hosted setup, 98.6% of calls < 800ms 99th percentile, and a production rollout after 10 weeks.
- Artifacts to share: anonymized latency graph, cost-per-1k tokens table, and a short quote from the customer engineering lead.

Security & technical FAQ (short answers for prospect meetings)
Q: Can Redwood run entirely within our VPC/on-prem?
A: Yes. Redwood Private provides a customer-managed control plane and an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging are included in the Private bundle.

Q: How do you handle key management and audit trails?
A: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and can use HSM-backed key stores for Private deployments. Audit logs are retained per contract and can be shipped to the customer SIEM.

Q: What happens to secrets and user data in hosted mode?
A: Hosted API supports request-level redaction policies and tokenization patterns. For sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private deployments and bring-your-own-key (BYOK) where keys never leave customer control.

Q: How do you prove model output stability during rollouts?
A: We support eval hooks and can run a customer-supplied prompt set in canary environments. Redwood Optimize provides regression alerts that flag statistical shifts vs a baseline prompt set prior to traffic percentage increases.

Q: What are typical SLAs for Dedicated?
A: Typical Dedicated SLAs include 99.9% uptime for the inference control plane and SLOs for median and p95 latency tailored by model family; specific numbers are in the negotiated contract.

Attachment checklist (what to include when you send to an integration architect)
- One-slide technical scorecard (PDF)
- Sample SDK snippet and rollout.yaml (text)
- Pilot proposal (term, included credit, acceptance criteria)
- Anonymized latency and cost graphs from an analogous customer
- Short security factsheet (one pager)

Owner and next steps
- Primary owner: Jordan Kim (SE lead) — jordan.kim@redwood.ai
- Suggested next steps: 1) Share this playbook before the architecture call, 2) prepare a one-page pilot proposal tailored to the customer’s QPS and latency targets, 3) bring the security factsheet if the customer is evaluating Private.

Appendix: sample rollout snippet (YAML, illustrative)
- name: fraud-scoring-rollout
  models:
    - id: open-quantized-small-v2
      weight: 70
    - id: optimized-medium-latency
      weight: 30
  canary:
    traffic_percent: 5
    duration: 2m
  fallback_policy: serve-compatible-variant

End of document.
